svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Metadata defenses, sorted by whether you will still be doing them
svg.desc: Three columns. The first holds defenses that work and that you will sustain, because they are decisions made once: choosing a provider that retains little, separating identities, routing traffic, and not creating the pattern in the first place. The second holds defenses that work in principle but depend on continuous human effort, such as randomising send times and varying your active hours. The third holds defenses that are frequently recommended and that individuals cannot deliver, principally cover traffic. A band below explains the practical conclusion.
svg.text: Figure 3: Sorted by Whether You Will Still Be Doing It
Most metadata advice is technically correct and behaviourally impossible. That distinction matters more than the technical detail.
works, and survives a busy week

g.text: Pick a provider that keeps little
The single largest change available, and it
is one decision.
Separate your identities
Different account for different work, so the
social graph never joins up.
Route the traffic
The only thing that addresses the network
column from Figure 1.
Do not create the pattern
Move the standing weekly call off a channel
that is being watched, rather than trying to
disguise it while it happens.

svg.text: works in principle, fails in practice

g.text: Randomise when you send
Correct, and it means holding a message you
have written and want to send. People do
this for a fortnight.
Vary your active hours
Correct, and it asks you to work at times
you would not otherwise work, indefinitely,
for a benefit you cannot observe.
Delete after reading
Genuinely useful, and the one item in this
column that automation can carry for you.
Set a timer rather than relying on habit.
Move what you can into column one.
Cover traffic
Sending decoy messages so the real ones do
not stand out. This has to be built into the
protocol and paid for in bandwidth by
everybody. An individual cannot add it, and
no mainstream messenger does it.
Padding message sizes
Same problem. It is a property of the
protocol, not a setting you enable.
Defeating a global observer
Somebody who can watch both ends of a
connection can correlate them. This is a
stated limit of anonymity networks, not a
gap in your configuration.

svg.text: The practical conclusion, and it is not the one most guides reach
You cannot obscure the shape of your communications by trying harder. What you can do is make the shape uninteresting: fewer distinct patterns, fewer
links between identities, and less that has to be defended at all. Column one does that with decisions. Column two asks for vigilance you will not sustain.
Lesson 1.4 said a control you abandon protected nothing. Column two is where that happens most often, and where the advice sounds most rigorous.
Spend your effort in column one, automate what you can from column two, and stop reading column three as a personal failing.
